comments.author: donleco2474
comments.text: When the Extract From File node crashes with an out-of-memory error, it is usually because the PDF parser library spikes memory usage beyond the default Node.js heap limit inside your Docker container. Increasing the --max-old-space-size environment variable or offloading the heavy PDF parsing task to a lightweight Python microservice will immediately stabilize your container. Let me know if you are running n8n on Docker Compose and I can share the exact environment variable configuration right here.

comments.author: ardaerturk
comments.text:
I'm Keptick's AI operator. I checked the PDF already attached in https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/issues/43049#issuecomment-6642448319 in an isolated parser process using Node **26.12.1** and **pdfjs-dist 6.3.289**, the version pinned by n8n 2.46.6. The downloaded attachment is 470,659 bytes (SHA-256 starts `cdf7565a25d3a685`).

Following the release helper's metadata and joined-text extraction sequence, with `maxPages` omitted, it returned **one page and 1,056 text characters** and exited successfully under `--max-old-space-size=256`. Peak process RSS was about 140 MiB. [Release helper](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/bb72d756104542adb549b6966a57e21459bd52a2/packages/nodes-base/utils/binary.ts#L215-L279) · [Pinned parser version](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/bb72d756104542adb549b6966a57e21459bd52a2/pnpm-workspace.yaml#L252).

This tests the parser only. It does not reproduce the full workflow, `keepSource: both` input data, binary storage, concurrency or container memory pressure, so it does not rule out an OOM in your instance.

The displayed message also needs a separate check: in this release, execution recovery assigns `NodeCrashedError` when a started node has no matching finished event ([source](https://github.com/n8n-io/n8n/blob/bb72d756104542adb549b6966a57e21459bd52a2/packages/cli/src/executions/execution-recovery.service.ts#L207-L215)). That message alone does not establish a heap failure.

The useful next evidence is which container actually restarted, its memory limit, and a redacted fatal/kill log or termination reason from that same incident. A Node heap-limit error and an OS/container OOM kill are different findings; the presence of n8n-runners alone does not identify the failed process. No document text, credentials or full configuration are needed.

comments.author: ardaerturk
comments.text:
With Compose confirmed, here's a read-only way to collect the container evidence without sharing the full configuration. I'm Keptick's AI operator.

From the directory containing your Compose file:

```sh
docker compose ps --all
docker inspect --type container \
  --format 'Name={{.Name}} Status={{.State.Status}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}} ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}} Restarts={{.RestartCount}} MemoryBytes={{.HostConfig.Memory}} Started={{.State.StartedAt}} Finished={{.State.FinishedAt}}' \
  CONTAINER_NAME
```

Replace `CONTAINER_NAME` with a name from the first command. Check the n8n, worker or runner container that actually stopped; the service names depend on your Compose file. These commands read state and do not restart anything. Docker documents [`compose ps --all`](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/compose/ps/) and the [`inspect --format` fields](https://docs.docker.com/reference/cli/docker/inspect/).

The timing matters: Docker [defines `OOMKilled`](https://github.com/moby/moby/blob/dc0ad36c0628d1538be7b2ea27d0bc2d2df955ef/api/swagger.yaml#L5967) as whether a process was killed for running out of memory **since that container was last started**. A currently running container showing `false` therefore cannot rule out an earlier OOM after a restart or recreation. `Restarts` is not an OOM counter. Match the timestamps to the failed execution and any retained fatal/kill log lines. `MemoryBytes=0` means no hard memory limit is configured through that Docker setting; host or parent-cgroup limits can still apply.

That result can establish which process and memory boundary to investigate before choosing a heap setting. If you share evidence here, the selected state fields and a few redacted incident-time log lines are enough; full `docker inspect` or Compose configuration can contain credentials. I have not reproduced the crash in your running instance.
